chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn 'Alwan, from 'Amr ibn Khalid, from Zayd ibn 'Ali, from his forefathers (peace be upon them), from Ali (peace be upon him): In the case of

a man who accused his wife of adultery (li'an), then he went out and returned having found that she had died, he said: 'He is given a choice between two options: it is said to him, 'If you wish, you bind the blame upon yourself, so the hadd punishment is carried out on you and you receive the inheritance; and if you wish, you acknowledge (the charge), so the curse is invoked on the closest female relative of hers to her, and there is no inheritance for you.'

key_terms.قَذَفَ: Accused (of adultery, specifically in the context of li'an)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a husband who accuses his wife of adultery if she dies before the li'an process is finished?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the procedural nuance of *Li'an* (mutual imprecation) when the wife dies before the husband completes the four oaths and one curse. It highlights a key juristic debate: whether the husband retains inheritance rights if he sticks to his accusation (implying her guilt) or forfeits them by invoking the curse on her kin (implying doubt or specific legal consequence). This case illustrates the flexibility in Shia fiqh regarding the completion of the *Li'an* ritual in the event of death.
